# Overview

This challenge is completed by the whole class as **one team of five**, on your own schedule, and it is the graded
portion of the version control material. The analysis is short. The learning goal is the workflow that collaborative
data teams use: forking, cloning, branching, committing, merging, resolving a conflict, and publishing a shared
history that shows who contributed what.

**The data question.** How did the number of attacks, the number of people killed, and the share of successful
attacks change across world regions and decades?

::: {.callout-note}
## Think About It

Before anyone writes code, the team meets once and answers the following. Which columns of the data does each part
of the question need? What should each intermediate object be called, so that five people writing in parallel
produce sections that fit together after the merge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reveal the discussion

The question needs `iyear` for time, `region_txt` for geography, `nkill` for fatalities, and `success` for the
outcome of the attack. A decade variable is derived from `iyear`. Agreeing in advance on object names and on the
columns that each object contains is the interface between the roles. The names in the table below are fixed for
this challenge, so that no team time is spent negotiating them. The team still confirms that every member has read
the table.
:::

# Tiers

| Tier | Tasks |
|:-----|:------|
| Floor | Fork, clone, create a role branch, commit twice, and push the branch. |
| Core | Merge the five branches into `main`, resolve the conflict, run the script from top to bottom, add the interpretation to the README, and push. |
| Stretch | Open a pull request to the instructor repository, and use `git revert` on a commit that was deliberately wrong. |

The floor and core tiers are required. The stretch tier is optional and is credited as described in the grading
section.

# Roles

The team chooses a **repository owner** who creates the fork and performs the merges. The owner also holds one of
the five roles. Each role is held by one member and works only in the region of the files assigned to it.

| Role | Branch name | Responsibility | Object or file produced |
|:-----|:------------|:---------------|:------------------------|
| 1: Wrangling | `role1-wrangle` | Keep rows with a valid `iyear`, keep the columns the team needs, and create a `decade` column | `gtd_clean` |
| 2: Summary | `role2-summary` | For each region and decade, count attacks, total the fatalities with `na.rm = TRUE`, and compute the share of successful attacks | `gtd_summary` |
| 3: Plot | `role3-plot` | Draw attacks per decade with one line for each region, with labeled axes | `attacks_plot` |
| 4: Checks | `role4-checks` | Report the percentage of missing `nkill` values in each region, and add `stopifnot()` checks that protect the analysis | `gtd_checks` |
| 5: Documentation | `role5-docs` | Write the research question and a data dictionary in the README, and later the interpretation of the results | `README.md` |

## The Interface Between Roles

The five sections are written at the same time, so each one assumes the objects that come before it.

| Object | Created by | Contents |
|:-------|:-----------|:---------|
| `gtd_clean` | Role 1 | Columns `iyear`, `region_txt`, `country_txt`, `attacktype1_txt`, `nkill`, `success`, and `decade` (text such as `"1990s"`) |
| `gtd_summary` | Role 2 | One row per region and decade, with columns `region_txt`, `decade`, `n_attacks`, `total_killed`, and `success_rate` |
| `attacks_plot` | Role 3 | A ggplot object built from `gtd_summary` |
| `gtd_checks` | Role 4 | One row per region, with columns `region_txt` and `pct_missing_nkill` |

Because the sections are written in parallel, a member cannot run their code until the branches are merged. A
member who wants to test earlier defines the object it depends on at the Console, which is not saved in the script,
or waits until the integration step and corrects any mismatch with one more commit.

# Planning and Timeline

All dates are set by the instructor in the email that accompanies this document.

| Milestone | What must be true |
|:----------|:------------------|
| Team confirmed | Each member has claimed one role, and the repository owner is named |
| Repository ready | The owner has forked the instructor repository and added the four teammates and the instructor as collaborators, and each teammate has accepted the invitation and cloned the fork |
| Branches pushed | Each member has at least two commits on their role branch, pushed to the fork |
| Integrated | The owner has merged all five branches into `main`, resolved the conflict, and pushed, and Role 5 has added the interpretation |
| Submitted | The fork link is emailed to the instructor |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ask for Help Before the Deadline

Authentication is where most first attempts stall. A member who cannot sign in to GitHub emails the instructor the
exact error message and the output of the five diagnostic commands in the lecture notes (`git --version`,
`git config --global --list`, `git remote -v`, `git status`, and `git log --oneline --graph --all`) as soon as the
problem appears, and does not wait for the final milestone.
:::

# Step A: Team Setup (floor)

1. **The owner forks.** The owner opens the instructor repository on GitHub and clicks **Fork** in the upper-right
   corner. This creates a copy under the owner's account.
2. **The owner invites.** Under Settings > Collaborators, the owner adds the four teammates and the instructor.
   **Each invited person accepts the invitation**, which arrives by email and also appears at
   `github.com/OWNER/REPO/invitations`.
3. **Everyone clones the fork**, not the instructor repository: File > New Project > Version Control > Git in
   RStudio, with the **HTTPS** URL copied from the fork page.
4. **The owner publishes the starter script** so that all five members begin from the same file.

```{bash}
#| label: team-start
cp analysis_template.R team_analysis.R                   # owner only: copy the starter script, then...
git add team_analysis.R                                  # stage the new file, then...
git commit -m "Add team analysis script from template"   # record it, then...
git push                                                 # publish to the fork, after which teammates run git pull
```

**Check.** `git log --oneline` shows the same latest commit identifier for all five members. A member whose log
differs runs `git pull`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why fork instead of clone?

A fork is an independent copy on GitHub where the team has write access, while the instructor repository stays
unchanged. Because the starter data and template are in the instructor repository, a fork gives the team those files
and a place to push without needing permission on the original.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## If This Fails: Step A

| Message or symptom | Usual cause | Fix |
|:-------------------|:------------|:----|
| `Repository not found` when cloning | The invitation has not been accepted, or the URL is mistyped | Accept the invitation, then clone again |
| `Permission to ... denied` on the first push | The project was cloned from the instructor repository, not the fork | Clone the fork, or run `git remote set-url origin` with the fork URL |
| A teammate's log does not match | The teammate has not pulled | `git pull` |
| The clone dialog fails with an authentication error | Stale credentials, or an SSH URL used without a key | Use the HTTPS URL and the HTTPS table in the lecture notes |
:::

The starter script has a contributor block, one marked section for each coding role, and a blank line between most
contributor lines. Role 5 writes in `README.md` and on the contributor line.

```{r}
#| label: starter-script
# Contributors
# Wrangling:
# Summary:

# Plot:

# Checks:

# Documentation:

library(tidyverse)
gtd <- read_csv("data/gtd_sample.csv")

# ---- Role 1: Wrangling ----

# ---- Role 2: Summary ----

# ---- Role 3: Plot ----

# ---- Role 4: Checks ----
```

# Step B: Parallel Development (floor)

Each member creates a branch with the name from the roles table, makes two commits, and pushes the branch.

1. Create the branch: `git switch -c role1-wrangle` (using the member's own branch name).
2. **First commit:** write the member's name on the matching contributor line, such as `# Wrangling: Alex`.
3. **Second commit:** write the role's code in its section. Role 5 writes the question and the data dictionary in
   `README.md`.
4. Push the branch: `git push -u origin role1-wrangle`.

The following code is an example of what the four coding sections can contain for this question. The team is
welcome to improve on it, provided the object names and columns from the interface table are kept.

```{r}
#| label: example-sections
# ---- Role 1: Wrangling ----
gtd_clean <- gtd %>%                                                   # start from the full table, then...
  filter(!is.na(iyear)) %>%                                            # drop rows without a year, then...
  select(iyear, region_txt, country_txt, attacktype1_txt,
         nkill, success) %>%                                           # keep the columns the team needs, then...
  mutate(decade = paste0(floor(iyear / 10) * 10, "s"))                 # label each year with its decade

# ---- Role 2: Summary ----
gtd_summary <- gtd_clean %>%                                           # start from the wrangled table, then...
  group_by(region_txt, decade) %>%                                     # one group for each region and decade, then...
  summarise(n_attacks = n(),                                           # number of attacks in the group
            total_killed = sum(nkill, na.rm = TRUE),                   # fatalities, ignoring missing values
            success_rate = mean(success == 1),                         # share of attacks coded as successful
            .groups = "drop")                                          # return an ungrouped table

# ---- Role 3: Plot ----
attacks_plot <- ggplot(gtd_summary,
                       aes(x = decade, y = n_attacks,
                           group = region_txt, colour = region_txt)) + # decade on x, one line per region, then...
  geom_line() +                                                        # connect the decades, then...
  labs(x = "Decade", y = "Number of attacks", colour = "Region")       # label the axes and the legend
attacks_plot                                                           # display the figure

# ---- Role 4: Checks ----
gtd_checks <- gtd_clean %>%                                            # start from the wrangled table, then...
  group_by(region_txt) %>%                                             # one group per region, then...
  summarise(pct_missing_nkill = mean(is.na(nkill)) * 100,              # percentage of missing fatality counts
            .groups = "drop")                                          # return an ungrouped table
stopifnot(!anyNA(gtd_clean$iyear), nrow(gtd_summary) > 0)              # stop with an error if a basic assumption fails
```

# Step C: Integration and Conflict (core)

The owner merges the five branches into `main`, in role order. The first merge is a fast-forward. The merge of the
Role 2 branch is expected to **conflict**, because the Wrangling and Summary contributor lines sit next to each other
and were edited on separate branches. The remaining contributor lines are separated by blank lines, so the merges of
Roles 3, 4, and 5 are expected to be clean.

```{bash}
#| label: integrate
git switch main                               # move to the integration branch, then...
git pull                                      # make sure main is current, then...
git fetch origin                              # download every teammate's pushed branch, then...
git merge --no-edit origin/role1-wrangle      # first merge, expected to fast-forward, then...
git merge --no-edit origin/role2-summary      # second merge, expected to report a conflict
```

Resolution follows four steps: open `team_analysis.R`, keep both contributor names, delete the lines that contain
`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`, then stage and commit.

```{bash}
#| label: resolve
git add team_analysis.R                                              # mark the file as resolved, then...
git commit -m "Merge role 2 summary and resolve contributor lines"   # complete the merge, then...
git merge --no-edit origin/role3-plot                                # third merge, expected to be clean, then...
git merge --no-edit origin/role4-checks                              # fourth merge, expected to be clean, then...
git merge --no-edit origin/role5-docs                                # fifth merge, expected to be clean, then...
git push                                                             # publish the integrated main to the fork
```

After the merges, the owner runs `team_analysis.R` from top to bottom. A script that does not run points to
mismatched object names or columns, which are corrected with one more commit. The four other members run `git pull`
on `main`. **Role 5** then writes the interpretation in the README: three to five sentences that describe what the
summary table and the figure show, and one sentence on what the missing-data check implies for the conclusions. Role
5 commits and pushes that change to `main`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## If This Fails: Step C

| Message or symptom | Usual cause | Fix |
|:-------------------|:------------|:----|
| `merge: role1-wrangle - not something we can merge` | The branch exists only on GitHub | Use `origin/role1-wrangle` after `git fetch origin`, as in the code above |
| No conflict appears | The merge order or the edits differ from the plan | This is acceptable. Describe in the README what happened, and continue |
| More conflicts than expected | Edits were made outside the assigned region | Resolve each file with the four steps, or run `git merge --abort` and agree on regions |
| A text editor opens | A merge commit message is being edited | `Esc`, `:wq`, Enter in vim, or add `--no-edit` |
| `rejected` on the final push | A teammate pushed to `main` in the meantime | `git pull`, then push again |
| The script stops with an error about an object or a column | The sections disagree on a name | Compare the object names with the interface table, fix them, and commit |
:::

# Step D: Pull Request and Revert (stretch)

1. On the fork page on GitHub, click **Contribute**, then **Open pull request**. The base is the instructor
   repository's `main` and the compare branch is the fork's `main`.
2. The description states each member's contribution in one sentence.
3. **Revert practice.** The owner commits a deliberately wrong change, pushes it, and then undoes it with
   `git revert HEAD` followed by `git push`. The README notes which commit was reverted.

# What to Submit

The team submits **one email** to the instructor by the final deadline, containing the link to the fork. The
instructor was added as a collaborator in Step A. Nothing else needs to be attached, because everything is graded
from the repository.

The repository on `main` contains the following.

- `team_analysis.R`, which runs from top to bottom and produces `gtd_clean`, `gtd_summary`, `attacks_plot`, and
  `gtd_checks`.
- `README.md`, with the question, the data dictionary, the interpretation, the name of the owner, and the role and
  branch of each member.
- The five role branches, left on GitHub and not deleted, so that the history shows who did what.

# Grading

Grading uses the repository history, which shows the contribution of each person.

| Component | What is checked | Weight |
|:----------|:----------------|:-------|
| Individual contribution | The member's own branch contains at least two commits under the member's name, with messages that describe the change | 40% |
| Collaboration workflow | All five branches were merged into `main`, the conflict is visible in the history together with its resolution, and every member's name is in the contributor block | 25% |
| Analysis | The script runs, the objects match the interface table, and the figure is labeled | 20% |
| README | The question, the data dictionary, and an interpretation that is supported by the results | 15% |

The individual contribution mark is assigned to each member separately. The other components are shared by the team.
The stretch tier earns up to 5 additional percentage points, divided as the instructor sees fit, for a pull request
with a clear description and a documented revert.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How a contribution is verified

The instructor runs `git log --oneline --graph --all` to confirm the branch and merge structure, and
`git shortlog -sn --all` to count commits by author. A commit is credited to the name and email in the author field,
which is set by the identity configured in Git on the computer that made the commit.
:::

# If Authentication Cannot Be Fixed

A member does not need to wait on one sign-in problem, and the instructor would rather receive an email than a
missed milestone. The options, in order of preference, are the following.

1. **Browser sign-in.** A computer with Git Credential Manager, or VS Code with its GitHub sign-in, can push without
   a token or an SSH key. VS Code is an acceptable tool for any Git step in this challenge.
2. **Pair at a working computer.** A teammate runs the commands while the member directs. The member's own work is
   credited correctly by committing with the member's identity:
   `git commit --author="Full Name <email-used-on-github>" -m "message"`.
3. **Local first.** Branching, committing, and merging do not need GitHub, so the member completes the branch
   locally and pushes after the sign-in is repaired.

# Reference

| Action | Command |
|:-------|:--------|
| Show the remote URL and protocol | `git remote -v` |
| Change the remote URL | `git remote set-url origin <url>` |
| Create and switch to a branch | `git switch -c branch-name` |
| Stage a file | `git add filename.R` |
| Commit | `git commit -m "message"` |
| Push a branch for the first time | `git push -u origin branch-name` |
| Download every branch from GitHub | `git fetch origin` |
| Merge a branch into the current branch | `git merge --no-edit branch-name` |
| Abandon a merge in progress | `git merge --abort` |
| Undo a pushed commit | `git revert HEAD` |
| View the history of all branches | `git log --oneline --graph --all` |
